list.listitem: Neonatal jaundice occurs in a majority of infants and is generally benign. A
All infants should be evaluated to identify those at risk of developing severe hyperbilirubinemia and neurotoxicity from hyperbilirubinemia: acute bilirubin encephalopathy or kernicterus. C

Physical examination is unreliable in assessing jaundice. Further assessment with total serum bilirubin (TSB) or transcutaneous bilirubin (TcB) should be done in the presence of visible jaundice and risk factors for severe hyperbilirubinemia. C
Once TSB or TcB is measured, the result should be applied to a clinical nomogram to determine the need for further evaluation and treatment. C

background.definition: Hyperbilirubinemia is defined as a serum bilirubin level of greater than 5 mg/dL. Severe hyperbilirubinemia is defined as a serum bilirubin level greater than 95th percentile for hours-of-age. Bilirubin-induced neurologic dysfunction (BIND) occurs when bilirubin crosses the blood-brain barrier and binds to brain tissue. Severe hyperbilirubinemia, especially as the serum bilirubin level reaches 25 to 30 mg/dL, places the infant at an increased risk for BIND. Premature infants of 34 or fewer weeks' gestation are at an increased risk for BIND at even lower serum bilirubin levels. Acute bilirubin encephalopathy describes the acute manifestations of bilirubin toxicity. Kernicterus describes the chronic and permanent sequelae of bilirubin toxicity.

list.listitem: Jaundice occurs in approximately 60% of newborns in the United States and typically peaks during the first 3 to 5 days of life. Bilirubin elevations > 20 mg/dL are uncommon: Total serum bilirubin (TSB) > 20 mg/dL (340 micromol/L): 2% TSB > 25 mg/dL (428 micromol/L): 0.14% TSB > 30 mg/dL (513 micromol/L): 0.01%
The rate of bilirubin-induced neurologic dysfunction is not well documented, but estimated at 1 in 133,000 infants.

Most hyperbilirubinemia is due to "physiologic jaundice," due to immaturity of the bilirubin metabolism pathways. This causes an unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia that tends to peak in the third day of life. Additional causes of unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia listed below are far less common and generally require intervention.
Blood group incompatibility: ABO, Rh, Kell, Duffy. Bruising from birth trauma, cephalohematoma. Sepsis. Pyloric stenosis. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. Congenital hypothyroidism. Crigler-Najjar syndrome. Gilbert syndrome. Breast milk jaundice due to other bilirubin UGT1A1 mutations. Galactosemia.

Intrahepatic or extrahepatic biliary obstruction causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (conjugated bilirubin level ≥20% of the total serum bilirubin). Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia is always pathologic and requires intervention.
Neonatal hyperbilirubinemia is caused by increased bilirubin production, decreased bilirubin conjugation, or increased enterohepatic circulation.
Bilirubin is produced by the catabolism of hemoglobin.
Normally, bilirubin is conjugated by the liver into a form that can be excreted through the gastrointestinal tract.
Unconjugated bilirubin is toxic to brain tissue.

Many infants have physiologic jaundice because they have an increased red blood cell mass and shortened erythrocyte half-life, causing increased bilirubin production that overwhelms their bilirubin conjugation system. In addition, newborns have increased enterohepatic circulation.

list.listitem: Newborn infants should be evaluated every 8 to 12 hours for the presence of jaundice. C

Prior to discharge from the hospital, all infants should either have a TcB and/or TSB measured (and plotted on a nomogram, , , and ) and/or be assessed for the presence of jaundice and risk factors for severe hyperbilirubinemia. C
Infants who are jaundiced before 24 hours of life are at increased risk for severe hyperbilirubinemia and should have further evaluation with either TSB or TcB. C
All pregnant women should be tested for ABO and Rh (D) blood types and have a serum screen for unusual isoimmune antibodies. C
Newborn infants should be evaluated every 8 to 12 hours for the presence of jaundice.
Newborns who appear jaundiced in the first 24 hours of life or who appear excessively jaundiced for age should have TcB and/or TSB measurement.

Prior to discharge from the hospital, all infants should either have a TcB and/or TSB measured (and plotted on a nomogram) and/or be assessed for the presence of jaundice and risk factors for severe hyperbilirubinemia. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommends universal screening of all infants with either TcB/TSB measurement or clinical assessment.The United States Preventive Services Task Force, however, found insufficient evidence available to recommend routine screening of healthy infants for hyperbilirubinemia citing a lack of data that identifying and treating hyperbilirubinemia prevents kernicterus. A prospective study of over 1000 infants found that TcB/TSB at time of discharge combined with clinical risk factors (earlier gestational age, bruising, positive direct antiglobulin test, Asian race, exclusive breastfeeding, blood type incompatability, jaundice extent) predicted subsequent phototherapy use (AUC = 95%; 95% CI: 93-97%).
All newborns discharged from the hospital should have follow-up examination(s) ().
Parents should feed their infants at least 8 to 12 times per day for the first several days.
Parents should not routinely supplement nondehydrated breast-fed infants with water or dextrose water.
Prior to discharge from the hospital, all parents should receive verbal information on how to monitor their baby for jaundice and when to return for follow-up.
All pregnant women should be tested for ABO and Rh (D) blood types and have a serum screen for unusual isoimmune antibodies.
If a mother has not had prenatal blood grouping or is Rh-negative, a direct antibody test (or Coombs' test), blood type, and an Rh (D) type on the infant's (cord) blood are strongly recommended.

If the maternal blood group is O, Rh-positive, you can test the cord blood for the infant's blood type and perform an antibody test directly, but it is not required provided there is appropriate surveillance, risk assessment before discharge, and follow-up.

Infants with serum bilirubin above the 95th percentile or with a clinical picture suggestive of hemolytic disease should have additional laboratory testing including: blood type and direct Coombs' test; complete blood count and smear; reticulocyte count; G6PD measurement, if clinically appropriate; direct or conjugated bilirubin; and ETCOc (if available).
If jaundice occurs in the first 24 hours of life the bilirubin level should be assessed using either TSB or TcB. C
Bilirubin levels should be measured using either TcB or TSB. TSB should be measured (instead of TcB) if the bilirubin level is expected to be greater than 15 mg/dL. C
The bilirubin level should be plotted on a nomogram by hours of life to determine the risk of severe hyperbilirubinemia. C

Exclusively breastfed, jaundice after the first 24 hours, peaks on days 3-4 (before breastmilk in)
Exclusively breastfed, jaundice after days 4-7 of life, peaks on day 14
Jaundice within the first 24 hours of life; ABO, Rh (or other blood type) incompatibility
Temperature instability, lethargy, irritability, poor feeding
Family history of G6PD or ethnic background of potential G6PD, slow response to phototherapy
Jaundice within the first 24 hours of life; slow response to phototherapy
Yellow/green skin color; jaundice noted after day 14
Older infant (eating foods high in beta-carotene: carrots, sweet potatoes, spinach); nonicteric sclera

list.listitem: The literature is conflicting on the accuracy of the physical examination in identifying the extent of neonatal hyperbilirubinemia.

Several papers concluded that finding no jaundice caudal to the nipple line will reliably predict a bilirubin level of less then 12 mg/dL, but at higher bilirubin levels the physical examination was less accurate.

Perhaps the most careful study to date recently had 5 neonatologists and 18 experienced nurses evaluate 1129 infants. The researchers found that physical exam was of limited value and often failed to identify infants with more severe hyperbilirubinemia.

TcB measurements of bilirubin have a linear correlation to TSB and may be useful as screening devices to detect clinically significant jaundice and decrease the need of serum bilirubin determinations. Smartphone app (BiliCam) was sensitive (84.6%-100%) and specific (75.1%-76%) in identifying neonates with hyperbilirubinemia when compared to TSB, with an overall 0.91 correlation in a diverse population.
TcB correlates well with TSB up to levels of 15 mg/dL, including in Hispanic, African, and multiethnic populations.
Transcutaneous devices are less accurate at higher levels of bilirubin.
Transcutaneous bilirubin measurement is not currently recommended in infants less than 35 weeks gestation.
TSB measurements should be done at higher bilirubin levels, in infants receiving phototherapy, and in any infant for whom the TcB level is not thought to be accurate.
All bilirubin measurements should be interpreted according to the infant's age in hours on the nomogram (see algorithm in and nomograms in and ).
Consider obtaining a urinalysis/urine culture in all infants with an elevated direct bilirubin level. Infants who appear sick should have a full rule-out sepsis work-up (ie, urine, blood, CSF).
Consider checking G6PD in infants with a positive family history, an ethnic background at high risk for G6PD, or a poor response to phototherapy.

Get a total/direct bilirubin measurement to check for cholestasis in infants older than 3 weeks with persistent jaundice. Also check the infant's newborn screening results for galactosemia and thyroid hormone level.

Initial laboratory tests for hospitalized patients: TSB; direct bilirubin; blood type (ABO, Rh); Coombs' test; albumin; CBC with differential and smear; reticulocyte count; end tidal carbon monoxide, if available; G6PD, if suggested by ethnic origin, family history, or poor response to phototherapy; and urine reducing substances.
A clinical decision rule has been developed that predicts the risk of hyperbilirubinemia on the basis of clinical risk factors and the initial bilirubin measurement.
The nomogram for treatment is also available as a clinical calculator.

A clinical prediction rule can quantify an infant's risk for rebound hyperbilirubinemia following inpatient phototherapy using gestational age and total serum bilirubin relative to the treatment threshold at phototherapy termination. Score = 15.5 (if gestational age <38 wks) − 4.3 x (AAP phototherapy threshold − Total serum bilirubin at phototherapy termination). If score <0, the infant has <5% chance of having rebound phototherapy and phototherapy may be terminated.
See the algorithm in and nomograms in , , and .
See and for guidance regarding initiation of therapy.

Routine supplementation of nondehydrated breast-fed infants with dextrose water is not recommended. C
Phototherapy and/or exchange tranfusion should be considered for infants on the basis of risk assessment using the appropriate nomogram (see and ). C

A clinical prediction rule can quantify an infant's risk for rebound hyperbilirubinemia following inpatient phototherapy using gestational age and total serum bilirubin relative to the treatment threshold at phototherapy termination. Score = 15.5 (if gestational age <38 wks) − 4.3 x (AAP phototherapy threshold − Total serum bilirubin at phototherapy termination). If score <0, the infant has <5% chance of having rebound phototherapy and phototherapy may be terminated. C

Metalloporphyrins, heme analogs that inhibit the production of bilirubin, may lower the maximum plasma bilirubin level, and may lower the frequency of severe hyperbilirubinemia. However, since long-term outcomes were not reported, routine treatment of unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with a metalloporphyrin is not recommended.

Clofibrate decreases peak bilirubin levels and duration of phototherapy required for severe hyperbilirubinemia, but there is insufficient evidence it decreases risk of bilirubin-induced neurologic dysfunction. There is also insufficient evidence of long-term safety of clofibrate in the treatment of neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, and therefore, routine use is not recommended.
Ursodiol also decreases peak bilirubin levels and duration of phototherapy without any immediate adverse effects, but more data on long-term safety and efficacy is needed.
Intravenous immunoglobulin has been used to treat alloimmune hemolytic anemia (Rh and ABO disease), but there is insufficient evidence it reduces the need for exchange transfusion.
See algorithm in .
Phototherapy is the first-line therapy for hyperbilirubinemia (). The need for phototherapy is based on an infant's gestational age in weeks, TSB, and neurotoxicity risk factors.

Keep neonates close to phototherapy lights (20 cm). There is a linear relationship between light irradiance and TSB; the closer an infant is to phototherapy between 20 and 47 cm, the larger the decrease in TSB in 24 hours.

Fiberoptic phototherapy is not as effective as traditional phototherapy. If 2 fiberoptic devices were used, it could have an additive effect to traditional phototherapy. There is no evidence that fiberoptic devices interfere less with infant care or parent-child bonding.
In areas where conventional phototherapy is unavailable, an RCT in African neonates found that filtered sunlight was non-inferior to conventional phototherapy.

A small (n=50) trial randomized neonates from 30 to 40 week gestation requiring phototherapy to usual care or phototherapy accompanied by kangaroo mother care (KMC) for 1 hour out of every 8. The duration of phototherapy was shorter in the KMC group (19 vs 39 hours, p < 0.05).

A trial randomized 280 preterm infants gestational age 28 to < 37 weeks to umbilical cord milking or delayed cord claimping at birth. There were no differences in neonatal hemoglobin, anemia, or maternal post-partum hemorrhage. However, neonatal jaundice was significantly less common in the umbilical cord milking group (6.8% vs 15.6%, p = 0.02).

Evidence is limited on the optimal time to discontinue phototherapy and expert recommendations vary. For infants older than 35 weeks' gestation who are readmitted for hyperbilirubinemia, phototherapy can generally be discontinued once the TSB level is less than 13 mg/dL.

Rebound hyperbilirubinemia is rare and routine monitoring of rebound bilirubin levels is not recommended. A rebound TSB level should be checked 24 hours after discontinuation of phototherapy in those infants whose phototherapy was discontinued before 4 days of age or was initiated early, or in infants with hemolytic disease.
Hospitalize the patient when intensive phototherapy or exchange transfusion is required.

Some infants with hyperbilirubinemia may be managed with outpatient phototherapy. However, outpatient phototherapy does not provide intensive phototherapy and should be reserved for infants in the "optional phototherapy" group. See nomograms in and .

Infants with a bilirubin level at or above the exchange transfusion level () should be admitted immediately to receive intensive phototherapy until an exchange transfusion can be performed at a neonatal intensive care unit.

Initial laboratory tests for hospitalized patients: TSB; direct bilirubin; blood type (ABO, Rh); Coombs' test; albumin; CBC with differential and smear; reticulocyte count; end tidal carbon monoxide, if available; G6PD, if suggested by ethnic origin, family history, or poor response to phototherapy; and urine reducing substances.

Utilize to determine thresholds for initiating phototherapy in infants > 35 weeks gestational age, according to hour-specific TSB and neurotoxicity risk factors. Follow up TSB should be obtained within 6-8 hours of initiating phototherapy to ensure a downward trend.

For infants approaching exchange transfusion thresholds shown in , obtain a type and cross in preparation for exchange transfusion in case TSB does not decrease with intensive phototherapy. In these infants, follow TSB closely at least every 3 hours.
Once TSB is falling, follow up TSB every 8 to 12 hours.
All infants should be examined by a health care provider soon after discharge. The timing of follow-up visits for infants older than 35 weeks is shown in . C
Infants who have risk factors for severe hyperbilirubinemia should be seen sooner and more frequently. C
At the follow-up visit, the infant should be assessed for adequate intake (feeding pattern), weight, percent change from birthweight, voiding and stooling pattern, and jaundice. C
Infants with severe neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (which met criteria for exchange transfusion) are at risk for chronic auditory toxicity. B

algorithm.title: Hyperbilirubinemia Risk Nomogram by Hour-Specific Serum Total Bilirubin Concentration in Healthy Term and Near-Term Newborns.

footnotes.footnote: The red, blue, and green lines denote the 95th, 75th, and 40th percentiles, respectively. Risk zones are designated according to percentile: high (serum total bilirubin or STB 95th), high intermediate (95th >STB 75th), low intermediate (75th >STB 40th), and low (STB <40th). Infants with values in the high risk zone are at increased risk for the development of clinically significant hyperbilirubinemia requiring intervention.

From Bhutani VK, Johnson L, Sivieri EM. Predictive ability of a predischarge hour-specific serum bilirubin for subsequent significant hyperbilirubinemia in healthy term and near-term newborns. Pediatrics 1999;103:6-14.

footnotes.footnote: Nomogram showing 5th, 25th, 50th, 75th, and 95th percentile for transcutaneous bilirubin measurements. Data are based upon measurements from 9337 healthy term infants (gestational age 35 weeks). The number of infants studied at each interval is shown in parentheses.
From Maisels MJ, Kring E. Transcutaneous bilirubin levels in the first 96 hours in a normal newborn population of > or =35 weeks' gestation. Pediatrics 2006;117:1169-1173.

algorithm.title: Guidelines for Phototherapy in Hospitalized Infants of 35 or More Weeks’ Gestation.

footnotes.footnote: Use total bilirubin. Do not subtract direct reacting or conjugated bilirubin. Risk factors include isoimmune hemolytic diseases, G6PD deficiency, asphyxia, significant lethargy, temperature instability, sepsis, acidosis, or albumin <3.0 g/dL (if measured). For well infants 35-37 6/7 wk can adjust TSB levels for intervention around the medium risk line. It is an option to intervene at lower TSB levels for infants closer to 35 wks and at higher TSB levels for those closer to 37 6/7 wk. It is an option to provide conventional phototherapy in hospital or at home at TSB levels 2-3 mg/dL (35-50 mmol/L) below those shown but home phototherapy should not be used in any infant with risk factors. Note: These guidelines are based on limited evidence and the levels shown are approximations. The guidelines refer to the use of intensive phototherapy which should be used when the TSB exceeds the line indicated for each category. Infants are designated as "higher risk" because of the potential negative effects of the conditions listed on albumin binding of bilirubin, the blood-brain barrier, and the susceptibility of the brain cells to damage by bilirubin.
From American Academy of Pediatrics Subcommittee on Hyperbilirubinemia. Management of hyperbilirubinemia in the newborn infant 35 or more weeks of gestation. Pediatrics 2004;114:297-316.

algorithm.title: Guidelines for Exchange Transfusion in Infants 35 or More Weeks of Gestation.

footnotes.footnote: The dashed lines for the first 24 hours indicate uncertainty due to a wide range of clinical circumstances and a range of responses to phototherapy. Immediate exchange transfusion is recommended if infant shows signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy (hypertonia, arching, retrocollis, opisthotonos, fever, or high-pitched cry) or if TSB is ≥5 mg/dL (85 μmol/L) above these lines. Risk factors include isoimmune hemolytic disease, G6PD deficiency, asphyxia, significant lethargy, temperature instability, sepsis, acidosis. Measure serum albumin and calculate B/A ratio. Use total bilirubin. Do not subtract direct reacting or conjugated bilirubin. If infant is well and 35-37 6/7 wk (median risk), you can individualize TSB levels for exchange based on actual gestational age. Note that these suggested levels represent a consensus of most of the committee members but are based on limited evidence, and the levels shown are approximations. During birth hospitalization, exchange transfusion is recommended if the TSB rises to these levels despite intensive phototherapy. For readmitted infants, if the TSB level is above the exchange level, repeat TSB measurement every 2 to 3 hours and consider exchange if the TSB remains above the levels indicated after intensive phototherapy for 6 hours.
From American Academy of Pediatrics Subcommittee on Hyperbilirubinemia. Management of hyperbilirubinemia in the newborn infant 35 or more weeks of gestation. Pediatrics 2004;114:297-316.
